article.title: Book Review
glossary: * behaviourism: a branch of psychology which is concerned with observable behaviour.

items.sentence_raw: "Happiness is the ultimate goal because it is self-evidently good.
If we are asked why happiness matters we can give no further external reason.
It just obviously does matter."
This pronouncement by Richard Layard, an economist and advocate of 'positive psychology', summarises the beliefs of many people today.
For Layard and others like him, it is obvious that the purpose of government is to promote a state of collective well-being.

The only question is how to achieve it, and here positive psychology - a supposed science that not only identifies what makes people happy but also allows their happiness to be measured - can show the way.
Equipped with this science, they say, governments can secure happiness in society in a way they never could in the past.
It is an astonishingly crude and simple-minded way of thinking, and for that very reason increasingly popular.

Those who think in this way are oblivious to the vast philosophical literature in which the meaning and value of happiness have been explored and questioned, and write as if nothing of any importance had been thought on the subject until it came to their attention.
It was the philosopher Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832) who was more than anyone else responsible for the development of this way of thinking.
For Bentham it was obvious that the human good consists of pleasure and the absence of pain.

The Greek philosopher Aristotle may have identified happiness with self-realisation in the 4th century BC, and thinkers throughout the ages may have struggled to reconcile the pursuit of happiness with other human values, but for Bentham all this was mere metaphysics or fiction.
items.explain: Q28: The passage mentions Aristotle to show he had a different idea: he *'identified happiness with self-realisation'*, not just pleasure. This is used to contrast with Bentham's view that happiness is only *'pleasure and the absence of pain'*. So the reviewer uses Aristotle to suggest that happiness **may not be just pleasure and the absence of pain** — answer **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Without knowing anything much of him or the school of moral theory he established - since they are by education and intellectual conviction illiterate in the history of ideas - our advocates of positive psychology follow in his tracks in rejecting as outmoded and irrelevant pretty much the entirety of ethical reflection on human happiness to date.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says advocates of positive psychology are *'illiterate in the history of ideas'* and reject *'the entirety of ethical reflection on human happiness to date'*. This means they simply do not know about the important ideas they should be thinking about. So the reviewer's attitude is that **they are ignorant about the ideas they should be considering** — answer **D**.

items.sentence_raw: But as William Davies notes in his recent book "The Happiness Industry", the view that happiness is the only self-evident good is actually a way of limiting moral inquiry.
One of the virtues of this rich, lucid and arresting book is that it places the current cult of happiness in a well-defined historical framework.
Rightly, Davies begins his story with Bentham, noting that he was far more than a philosopher.
Davies writes, "Bentham's activities were those which we might now associate with a public sector management consultant".

In the 1790s, he wrote to the Home Office suggesting that the departments of government be linked together through a set of 'conversation tubes', and to the Bank of England with a design for a printing device that could produce unforgeable banknotes.
items.explain:
Q30: The passage says Bentham suggested *'conversation tubes'* to link government departments. **'Conversation'** is about talking, which is a form of **communication**. So the answer is **F**.

Q31: The passage says Bentham designed a printing device to make *'unforgeable banknotes'*. If banknotes cannot be forged, they are safe and have more **security**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: He drew up plans for a 'frigidarium' to keep provisions such as meat, fish, fruit and vegetables fresh.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says Bentham planned a *'frigidarium'* to keep food *'fresh'*. Keeping food fresh means stopping it from going bad, which is **preservation**. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: His celebrated design for a prison to be known as a 'Panopticon', in which prisoners would be kept in solitary confinement while being visible at all times to the guards, was very nearly adopted.
items.explain: Q33: The passage describes the Panopticon prison where prisoners were *'visible at all times to the guards'*. Being visible means they were under constant **observation**. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: (Surprisingly, Davies does not discuss the fact that Bentham meant his Panopticon not just as a model prison but also as an instrument of control that could be applied to schools and factories.)
Bentham was also a pioneer of the 'science of happiness'.
If happiness is to be regarded as a science, it has to be measured, and Bentham suggested two ways in which this might be done.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says for happiness to be a science, *'it has to be measured'*, and Bentham suggested ways to do this. So he investigated possibilities for its **measurement** — answer **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Viewing happiness as a complex of pleasurable sensations, he suggested that it might be quantified by measuring the human pulse rate.
Alternatively, money could be used as the standard for quantification: if two different goods have the same price, it can be claimed that they produce the same quantity of pleasure in the consumer.
Bentham was more attracted by the latter measure.

By associating money so closely to inner experience, Davies writes, Bentham "set the stage for the entangling of psychological research and capitalism that would shape the business practices of the twentieth century".
items.explain: Q29: Davies says Bentham's idea of linking money to happiness *'set the stage for the entangling of psychological research and capitalism'*. **'Entangling'** means connecting two things together. So this idea was significant because **it established a connection between work and psychology** — answer **B**.

items.sentence_raw: "The Happiness Industry" describes how the project of a science of happiness has become integral to capitalism.
We learn much that is interesting about how economic problems are being redefined and treated as psychological maladies.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says the book shows how economic problems are treated as *'psychological maladies'* and how measuring feelings has *'informed management studies and advertising'*. This is a clear discussion of the link between psychology and economics. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: In addition, Davies shows how the belief that inner states of pleasure and displeasure can be objectively measured has informed management studies and advertising.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says the book shows how economic problems are treated as *'psychological maladies'* and how measuring feelings has *'informed management studies and advertising'*. This is a clear discussion of the link between psychology and economics. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: The tendency of thinkers such as J B Watson, the founder of behaviourism*, was that human beings could be shaped, or manipulated, by policymakers and managers.
Watson had no factual basis for his view of human action.
When he became president of the American Psychological Association in 1915, he 'had never even studied a single human being': his research had been confined to experiments on white rats.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says Watson *'had never even studied a single human being'* before 1915 — his research was only on *'white rats'*. So the statement that his ideas were supported by research on humans is directly contradicted. The answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Yet Watson's reductive model is now widely applied, with 'behaviour change' becoming the goal of governments: in Britain, a 'Behaviour Insights Team' has been established by the government to study how people can be encouraged, at minimum cost to the public purse, to live in what are considered to be socially desirable ways.
Modern industrial societies appear to need the possibility of ever-increasing happiness to motivate them in their labours.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says *'Modern industrial societies appear to need the possibility of ever-increasing happiness to motivate them'*. This directly links the need for happiness to industrialisation. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: But whatever its intellectual pedigree, the idea that governments should be responsible for promoting happiness is always a threat to human freedom.
items.explain: Q40: The passage states that the idea of governments promoting happiness is *'always a threat to human freedom'*. This means the reviewer thinks it is a bad idea, not a main aim. So the answer is **NO**.

subtitles: The Happiness Industry: How the Government and Big Business Sold Us Well-Being

orphan_explain_map.36: Q36: The passage talks about measuring happiness and inner states, but it never compares the difficulty of measuring different emotions. There is no information about one emotion being harder to measure than another. So the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
orphan_explain_map.38: Q38: The passage mentions a British government team using Watson's ideas, but it never says whether governments outside America were *most* influenced. We don't know if American or other governments were influenced more. So the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
